title: Week 2 review: log-processing challenge
goal: Answer real questions about a production access log with grep, sed, awk, sort and uniq, then wrap the pipeline in a reusable function.
setup: # access log of the to-do app: ip - - [time] "METHOD PATH HTTP/1.1" status bytes ms "user-agent"
# P4: the same log under a name with a space, and a broken report script

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Usage: report.sh <logfile> [top-n]   (top-n is optional, default 3)' '# Prints the top N paths, then the average response time in ms (field 11).' 'top_paths() {' '  awk '"'"'{print $7}'"'"' $1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n "$2"' '}' 'avg_ms() {' '  return $(awk '"'"'{s += $11} END {print int(s / NR)}'"'"' "$1")' '}' 'LOG=$1' 'N=$2' 'top_paths "$LOG" "$N"' 'avg_ms "$LOG"' 'echo "average: $? ms"' > report.sh

warmup.q: How do you get the file name from `$path` with parameter expansion?
Which grep options print only the matching part with extended regex?
How does a function return a string?
warmup.a: It prints it with `echo`; the caller uses `VAR=$(func)`.

warmup.q: What is the safe way to read a file line by line?
warmup.a: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`

problems.title: Challenge 1: clean the log (grep + sed)
problems.situation: The to-do app's `access.log` is full of Kubernetes health checks (user agent `kube-probe`). They hide the real traffic. Also, paths like `/api/todos/15` should count as one endpoint `/api/todos/:id`. Build a clean file for the next challenges.
task: Count the lines of `access.log`, and count the `kube-probe` lines.
Remove the probe lines with `grep -v`.
In the same pipeline, replace a number at the end of an API path with `:id` using `sed -E`.
Save the result as `clean.log`, count its lines, and show its first 3 lines.
hints: `sed -E 's#(/api/[a-z]+)/[0-9]+ #\1/:id #'` (with `#` as delimiter, because the text has `/`).

explanation.meaning: Remove health-check noise (Day 2 and 10).
Extended regex substitute with `#` as delimiter (Day 11).
Group 1 is `/api/todos`; then a slash, digits and a space.
Keep group 1, add `/:id`.
Continue the pipeline on the next line, for readability.
Stop after the first match.

mistakes: Forgetting the space after `[0-9]+` in the pattern: it also changes `/api/todos/15/items` paths in bigger logs.
Writing the result to `access.log` itself (`> access.log`): the file is emptied before grep reads it.
problems.interview_say: First I remove noise like health checks with `grep -v`, then I normalise ids in paths with `sed -E`, so the next counts group the same endpoint together.
problems.try_yourself: Also normalise user ids and count how many different endpoints are left: `awk '{print $7}' clean.log | sort -u | wc -l`.

problems.title: Challenge 2: status classes and error rate (awk)
problems.situation: The team lead asks for the health of the API in numbers: how many 2xx, 4xx and 5xx responses, and the 5xx error rate in percent. Use `clean.log` (run Challenge 1 first, or copy its command).
task: Find the field number of the status code (count the fields of one line, or use `awk '{print $9}'`).
Count the responses per class (`2xx`, `4xx`, `5xx`) with an awk array and `substr($9, 1, 1)`.
Print the 5xx error rate with one decimal in `END`.
Print the 5xx lines: time, path and response time only.
hints: Fields: 1 ip, 4 time, 6 method, 7 path, 9 status, 11 ms.
`substr($9, 1, 1)` = the first character of the status: 2, 4 or 5.
solution: [ -f clean.log ] || grep -v kube-probe access.log | sed -E 's#(/api/[a-z]+)/[0-9]+ #\1/:id #' > clean.log
awk '{ c[substr($9, 1, 1) "xx"]++ } END { for (k in c) print k, c[k] }' clean.log | sort
awk '$9 >= 500 { e++ } END { printf "5xx rate: %.1f%% of %d requests\n", e * 100 / NR, NR }' clean.log

explanation.meaning: First digit plus `xx`: the key becomes `2xx`, `4xx` or `5xx`.
Count per key in an awk array (Day 11).
awk does decimal math; NR in END is the number of lines.
Remove the `[` before the time (Day 12).
Create `clean.log` only if Challenge 1 was not done (Day 6).

problems.expected_output:
2xx 36
4xx 6
5xx 5
5xx rate: 10.6% of 47 requests
=== 5xx details ===
20/Oct/2026:10:00:09 /api/todos 1997 ms
20/Oct/2026:10:00:18 /api/todos 1774 ms
20/Oct/2026:10:00:27 /api/todos/:id 1551 ms
20/Oct/2026:10:00:45 /login 1805 ms
20/Oct/2026:10:00:54 /api/users/:id 1582 ms
mistakes: Using `$8` for the status: the method field `"GET` makes the count shift. Always check the field numbers on one line first.
Dividing with bash `$(( ))`: it gives a whole number (0 or 7), not 7.6.
problems.interview_say: I group status codes by class with an awk array and compute the error rate in END. If the 5xx rate is high, I look at the 5xx lines and their paths and times.
problems.try_yourself: Compute the error rate for the original `access.log` too. Why is it lower there? (Hint: probes are always 200.)

problems.title: Challenge 3: top endpoints and the IPs behind errors
problems.situation: Product wants the most used endpoints. Security wants to know which clients get the most 5xx errors and which IP sends the most POST /login requests (a possible password-guessing attack).
task: Top 3 endpoints in `clean.log` with counts (`sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`).
IPs that received 5xx errors, with counts.
IPs that sent `POST /login`, with counts, biggest first.
solution: [ -f clean.log ] || grep -v kube-probe access.log | sed -E 's#(/api/[a-z]+)/[0-9]+ #\1/:id #' > clean.log
awk '{print $7}' clean.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
grep '"POST /login ' clean.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

explanation.meaning: The classic counting pipeline (Day 12), now on endpoints.
Filter and pick a field in one step.
Fixed text with the quote, method, path and a space: no false matches.

mistakes: Counting before normalising ids: `/api/todos/1`, `/2` and `/15` are counted as three different endpoints.
Using `head` before `sort -rn`: the result is the first lines of the file, not the top values.
problems.interview_say: To find top endpoints or suspicious clients, I filter with awk or grep, then use `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`.
problems.try_yourself: Find the endpoint with the most 404 responses.

problems.title: Find the bug: report.sh
problems.situation: A teammate turned the pipelines into `report.sh`. It works for `access.log` with a number, but `bash report.sh "web 1.log"` fails, and the average time it prints is far too small.
task: Run `bash report.sh "web 1.log"` (no second argument). Read the errors.
Run `bash report.sh access.log 3`. Compare the average with `awk '{s+=$11} END {print int(s/NR)}' access.log`.
Find 3 bugs: an unquoted variable, a missing default, and `return` used for data.
Fix them and run `bash report.sh "web 1.log"` again.
hints: The comment says top-n is optional with default 3: `N=${2:-3}`.
`return` keeps only 0-255. Print the average with `echo` and catch it with `$( )`.
solution: # Prints the top N paths, then the average response time in ms (field 11).

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: without quotes, awk got `web` and `1.log` as two files.
Bug 2: with no second argument, `head -n ""` failed.
Bug 3: `return 559` became 559 % 256 = 47. Data must be printed, not returned.
Bonus: stop with a usage message when no log file is given.

problems.expected_output:
awk: cannot open "web" (No such file or directory)
head: invalid number of lines: ‘’
average: 223 ms
--- correct average for comparison ---
479
--- fixed ---
     20 /api/todos
     12 /health
      9 /login
average: 479 ms
mistakes: Quoting only `$LOG` in the main part and forgetting `$1` inside the function. Every use needs quotes.
Thinking the small average is a data problem. A value that is always below 256 is a hint that `return` was used.
problems.interview_say: The three bugs I see most in bash reports are unquoted variables, missing defaults for optional arguments, and functions that use `return` for data. ShellCheck finds the first one.
problems.try_yourself: Add a third optional argument: the field number to report (default 7), and use `awk -v f="$3" '{print $f}'`.

problems.title: Convert the pipeline into a reusable function
problems.situation: The user typed `awk '{print $N}' file | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n K` many times today with different N and K. Make one function `top_n FIELD COUNT FILE` and use it three times.
task: Write `top_n()` with three arguments: field number, how many lines, and the file. Use `local` variables.
Check that the field and count are numbers; if not, print a usage message to stderr and `return 2`.
Use it for: top 2 IPs, top 3 paths, and top status codes, on `access.log`.
Call it with a wrong field (`x`) and print the exit code.
hints: Pass the field to awk with `-v f="$field"` and print `$f`.
solution: awk -v f="$field" '{print $f}' "$file" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n "$count"

explanation.meaning: Name the arguments; keep them inside the function (Day 9).
Validate input with a regex (Day 6).
Pass a shell value into awk; `$f` is the field with that number.
Here `return` is right: it reports failure, not data.

problems.expected_output:
=== top 2 IPs ===
     15 192.168.1.20
     15 172.16.0.3
=== top 3 paths ===
     20 /api/todos
     12 /health
      9 /login
=== status codes ===
     48 200
      6 404
      5 500
usage: top_n FIELD COUNT FILE
exit code: 2
mistakes: Writing `awk '{print $'$field'}'`: it works, but quoting is hard to read and easy to break. `-v` is clearer.
Leaving the function's variables global: they can overwrite `count` or `file` in the caller.
problems.interview_say: When I repeat a pipeline, I turn it into a function with named local arguments, validate them, and pass values to awk with `-v`.
problems.try_yourself: Put `top_n` into a file `logtools.sh` and load it in a new terminal with `source logtools.sh`.

problems.title: Slowest endpoints: average time per path
problems.situation: Users say the app feels slow. The user computes the average response time per endpoint from `clean.log` and lists the slowest first, so the backend team knows where to look.
task: In awk, sum field 11 per path (field 7) and count requests per path.
In `END`, print `average path count` for each path.
Sort by the average, biggest first.
hints: `END { for (p in sum) printf "%6.0f %-16s %d\n", sum[p] / n[p], p, n[p] }`
solution: [ -f clean.log ] || grep -v kube-probe access.log | sed -E 's#(/api/[a-z]+)/[0-9]+ #\1/:id #' > clean.log
END { for (p in sum) printf "%6.0f ms  %-16s %d requests\n", sum[p] / n[p], p, n[p] }' clean.log | sort -rn

explanation.meaning: Total time and number of requests per path.
Average per path.
Number with no decimals, 6 wide, so `sort -rn` reads it as a number.

problems.expected_output:
606 ms  /login           9 requests
   500 ms  /api/todos/:id   12 requests
   482 ms  /api/todos       20 requests
   464 ms  /api/users/:id   6 requests
mistakes: Averages hide spikes. One 2000 ms request among fast ones looks fine on average. Also check the maximum or the 95th percentile.
problems.interview_say: I group by endpoint in awk with two arrays, sum and count, then print the average per endpoint and sort it. For real monitoring I would use percentiles in Prometheus or CloudWatch.
problems.try_yourself: Add the maximum time per path: `if ($11 > max[$7]) max[$7] = $11`.

interview.q: Rapid 1: How do you read a file line by line without losing backslashes?
interview.a: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`. `-r` keeps backslashes.

interview.q: Rapid 2: How do you create an associative array?

interview.a: `return` sets an exit code (0-255). `echo` prints data, caught with `$(func)`.
`"$@"` keeps each argument separate. `"$*"` joins them into one string.

interview.q: Rapid 5: grep for ERROR or FATAL, with 2 lines of context after?
Rapid 6: Replace every `http:` with `https:` in a file, in place, with a backup?
Rapid 7: Sum the 3rd column of a CSV?
Rapid 8: Find and delete `.tmp` files older than 3 days?
interview.a: `find /path -name '*.tmp' -mtime +3 -print` to check, then the same with `-delete`.

interview.q: Rapid 9: Top 5 IPs in an access log?
Rapid 10: File name from a path, and a date for a backup name?
